title: A plan for a lifetime
blurb: Two goals and an emergency fund, the payment that gets you there, RRSPs and tax, and checking a number you find online.

levels.title: Two goals, two plans
learn: Match a short-term goal and a long-term goal to different kinds of savings.
Work out how many months an emergency fund covers and say what it changes in a crash.

cards.text: A plan starts with a goal and a date. A short-term goal is under 5 years away, such as a used car in 3 years. A long-term goal is 20 years or more away, such as retirement. One person can have both, and two different dates call for two different plans.

Money for a short-term goal has little time to wait out a fall in value. It goes in a cash equivalent: a very safe place that turns into cash fast, such as a savings account. It grows slowly, but the amount you saved is still there on the day you need it.

Money for a long-term goal has time. Equities can fall, but a person decades from the goal has years to wait for the repair. So the long-term plan can lean toward equities. A good plan says in advance what to do when a fall comes, instead of deciding in a panic.

Before either goal comes an emergency fund: savings for a job loss, a repair or a bill nobody planned. A common target is 3 to 6 months of expenses. Months covered = fund / monthly expenses. Nia spends $2,400.00 a month and has $9,600.00 saved: 9,600 / 2,400 = 4.0 months.

Why first? Say Nia’s investments are worth $120,000.00 and a crash takes 15% off. That is a paper loss of $18,000.00. If she then loses her job, her fund pays the bills, and she does not have to sell investments while prices are down. Without the fund, a loss on paper could become a real one.

A plan also changes over a lifetime. As a goal gets closer there is less time to repair a fall, so a plan can lower its equities. Here is one made-up plan. Re-check your risk tolerance whenever life changes, such as a new job, a new home or a big expense.

questions.label: Short or long
questions.prompt: Mira needs money for a trip in 2 years. Her other goal is retirement, 38 years away. Which pairing is right?
questions.hint: Compare each date with 5 years and with 20 years.

options.text: The trip is short-term and retirement is long-term
options.why: The trip is under 5 years away, and retirement is 20 years or more away.

options.text: Both are long-term goals, because both need saving
options.why: A long-term goal is 20 years or more away. The trip is only 2 years away.

options.text: The trip is long-term and retirement is short-term
options.why: That swaps them. A short-term goal is under 5 years away.

questions.label: Trip money
questions.prompt: Following the plan on the cards, where does the money for Mira’s trip in 2 years belong?

terms.meaning: A very safe, short-term place that turns into cash fast, such as a savings account.

questions.hint: Ask how long the money can wait if the market falls.

options.text: In mostly equities, so it grows as much as possible
options.why: Equities can fall, and 2 years is not enough time to wait for the repair.

options.text: In a cash equivalent such as a savings account
options.why: Money needed soon cannot wait out a fall, so it goes somewhere very safe that turns into cash fast.

options.text: In the same long-term mix as retirement, to keep it simple
options.why: The trip is 2 years away and retirement is 38. Different dates need different plans.

questions.label: Six-month target
questions.prompt: Hal spends $2,375.00 a month. How many dollars is 6 months of his expenses?

terms.meaning: Savings kept for a job loss, a repair or a bill nobody planned.

questions.hint: Multiply one month of expenses by the number of months.
questions.why: The target is counted in months of expenses, so multiply one month by 6.
questions.miss: Take one month of expenses and multiply it by 6.

traps.why: That is 3 months. The question asks for 6.
That adds 6 dollars. Multiply by 6 instead.

questions.label: Months covered
questions.prompt: Kit spends $2,000.00 a month and has $9,000.00 in an emergency fund. How many months does the fund cover?

terms.meaning: Savings kept for a job loss, a repair or a bill nobody planned.

questions.hint: Divide the fund by one month of expenses.

options.text: 0.22 months
options.why: That divides the other way, expenses by fund. Divide the fund by the expenses.

options.text: 3 months
options.why: That is the low end of the usual target, not what this fund covers.

options.text: 4.5 months
options.why: 9,000 / 2,000 = 4.5. Months covered is the fund divided by one month of expenses.

questions.label: What the fund changes
questions.prompt: A crash cuts the value of Nell’s investments, and the same month her hours are cut. She has an emergency fund. What does the fund let her do?

terms.meaning: Savings kept for a job loss, a repair or a bill nobody planned.

questions.hint: Think about what she would have to sell without the fund.

options.text: Stop her investments from falling in value
options.why: The crash still happens. The fund changes what she has to do about it, not the prices.

options.text: Pay bills from it and leave her investments alone while prices are down
options.why: Yes. She does not have to sell at the low prices, so the loss stays on paper.

options.text: Sell her investments quickly before they fall more
options.why: That is the panic move the fund helps her avoid. It turns a paper loss into a real one.

questions.label: Paper loss
questions.prompt: Gil’s investments are worth $84,000.00. A crash takes 15% off. How many dollars is the paper loss?
questions.hint: Find 15% of the value: multiply by 0.15.
questions.why: A percent loss is that percent of the value before the fall.
questions.miss: Multiply the value before the crash by 0.15. The result is the amount lost.

traps.why: That is what is left after the crash, not the loss.

questions.label: Most months covered
questions.prompt: Four friends spend a different amount each month: Eve $1,500.00, Bo $2,500.00, Max $2,000.00 and Di $1,000.00. Each bar is that friend’s emergency fund. Tap the friend whose fund covers the most months.

terms.meaning: Savings kept for a job loss, a repair or a bill nobody planned.

questions.hint: Divide each friend’s fund by that friend’s monthly expenses.
questions.why: Months covered is fund / expenses. Di has 8,000 / 1,000 = 8 months. Bo has the biggest fund, but also the biggest bills.
questions.miss: Work out fund / expenses for each friend. The biggest bar is not always the most months.

questions.label: When life changes
questions.prompt: Abe’s plan worked for years. This year Abe starts a new job and takes on a large expense. What do the cards say about his risk tolerance?

terms.meaning: How big a fall in value a person can live with without being forced to sell or choosing to sell in a panic.

questions.hint: Look at the last card.

options.text: Re-check it, because his time and needs may have changed
options.why: Risk tolerance belongs to the person and can change as life changes, so it is worth re-checking.

options.text: Keep it, since a plan once made never needs a second look
options.why: The cards say to re-check it when life changes. A plan is not set once for good.

options.text: Raise it, because a new job always means more risk is fine
options.why: Nothing says it goes up. It may go down. It has to be re-checked, not guessed.

questions.label: Late-stage mix
questions.prompt: In the made-up plan, the late years hold 30% in equities. On $90,000.00, how many dollars are not in equities?
questions.hint: The rest of the money is 100% minus the share in equities.
questions.why: What is not in equities is the rest: 100% minus 30%, which is 70%.
questions.miss: First find the share that is not in equities, then take that share of the money.

traps.why: That is the part in equities. The question asks for the rest.

levels.title: The payment that gets you there
learn: Say what a regular payment is for, whether it pays off a loan or builds a goal.
Work out a payment with the formula and see how the time you allow changes it.

cards.text: A regular payment is the same amount every month, and it can do one of two jobs. It can pay off a loan: you borrow now and pay it back in equal parts. Or it can build a goal: you set aside the same amount each month until you reach a target. A spreadsheet has a payment function that finds it.

The payment function needs three things: the rate for one period, the number of periods and the amount. Class example: $20,000.00 borrowed at 6% a year, paid monthly for 10 years. The monthly rate is 6% / 12 = 0.5% and there are 120 months. The payment is $222.04. Over 5 years, it jumps.

Add up what is paid: $222.04 x 120 is about $26,645. The borrower got $20,000, so about $6,645 is interest, the cost of borrowing. It is the same compound growth that builds savings, now working against the borrower.

By hand, a loan payment is amount x r / (1 - (1 + r)^-n). Here r is the rate for one month and n the number of months. For the class loan, r = 0.005 and n = 120: 20,000 x 0.005 / (1 - 1.005^-120) = $222.04. A negative power means 1 divided by that power.

Saving toward a goal turns it around. With a deposit at the end of each month, deposit = goal x r / ((1 + r)^n - 1). In this example a savings account pays 3% a year, so r = 0.25% a month. To have $6,000.00 in 3 years (n = 36), the deposit is $159.49 a month.

Time changes the payment. For the same goal at the same rate, a longer wait means a smaller deposit, and more of the goal comes from interest. Here are three waits for the same $6,000.00 goal at the same 3%. The amounts paid in are the deposit times the months.

questions.label: Who earns interest
questions.prompt: Interest shows up in both jobs of a regular payment. Who earns it on a loan, and who earns it on a savings goal?
questions.hint: Look at the card on the cost of borrowing.

options.text: On a loan the lender earns it. On savings you earn it
options.why: A borrower pays interest as the cost of borrowing. A saver is paid interest on the money in the account.

options.text: On a loan you earn it. On savings the bank earns it
options.why: That is reversed. The borrower pays and the saver is paid.

options.text: You earn it both times, as the person making the payments
options.why: A borrower pays interest, so it is not earned on a loan.

questions.label: Monthly rate
questions.prompt: A savings account pays 4.8% a year in this example, and deposits go in monthly. What monthly rate, in percent, goes into the payment formula?
questions.hint: The formula uses the rate for one month. How many months are in a year?
questions.why: The formula works one month at a time, so the yearly rate is split over 12 months.
questions.miss: Divide the yearly rate by the number of months in a year.

traps.why: That multiplies. A month is a twelfth of a year, so divide.

questions.label: Loan payment
questions.prompt: Jun borrows $12,000.00 at 6% a year, paid monthly over 5 years (60 months, monthly rate 0.5%). What is her monthly payment, to the nearest cent?

terms.meaning: A spreadsheet tool that finds the regular payment from a rate for one period, a number of periods and an amount.

questions.hint: Use amount x r / (1 - (1 + r)^-n). Work out 1.005^-60 first.
questions.why: The payment covers the loan and its interest, so it is more than the loan divided by 60.
questions.miss: Use r = 0.005 and n = 60 in the loan formula. Keep the minus sign on the power.

traps.why: That is the loan divided by 60. It leaves out the interest.

questions.label: Goal deposit
questions.prompt: Ezra wants $9,000.00 in 4 years from an account paying 3% a year (monthly rate 0.25%, 48 months). Deposits go in at the end of each month. What monthly deposit does he need, to the nearest cent?

terms.meaning: A spreadsheet tool that finds the regular payment from a rate for one period, a number of periods and an amount.

questions.hint: Use goal x r / ((1 + r)^n - 1). Work out 1.0025^48 first.
questions.why: Interest does part of the work, so the deposit is less than the goal divided by the number of months.
questions.miss: Use r = 0.0025 and n = 48 in the goal formula. The power gets 1 taken away, not 1 added.

traps.why: That splits the goal over 48 months and ignores interest. The deposit needed is smaller.

questions.label: Longer or shorter
questions.prompt: Two plans reach the same goal at the same rate. Plan A takes 3 years and Plan B takes 6 years. Which has the smaller monthly deposit, and why?
questions.hint: Look at the table of three waits.

options.text: Plan A, because fewer months means less to pay
options.why: Fewer months means each deposit has to be bigger to reach the same goal.

options.text: They are the same, because the goal is the same
options.why: The goal is the same, but the deposits are not. Time changes the payment.

options.text: Plan B, because there are more months and interest does more of the work
options.why: More months share the goal among more deposits, and interest has longer to add to it.

questions.label: Shortest she can afford
questions.prompt: Each bar is the monthly deposit needed to reach $10,000.00 in an account paying 3% a year, over 2, 3, 4 or 5 years. Toni can set aside $200.00 a month. Tap the shortest plan she can afford.
questions.hint: Find the first bar that is no more than $200.00, starting from the shortest plan.
questions.why: The 4-year plan needs $196.34, which fits in $200.00. The shorter plan needs $265.81, which is too much.
questions.miss: The shortest plans need more than $200.00 a month. Find the first bar that fits.

questions.label: Cost of a loan
questions.prompt: Bao’s loan is $10,000.00 at 6% a year over 3 years. The payment is $304.22 a month for 36 months. How many dollars of interest does Bao pay in all?
questions.hint: Total paid is the payment times the months. Interest is what is above the loan.
questions.why: Interest is everything paid beyond the amount borrowed.
questions.miss: Multiply the payment by the number of months, then take off the amount borrowed.

traps.why: That is the total paid, which includes the $10,000.00 borrowed. Take the loan off to get the interest.

questions.label: A deposit too big
questions.prompt: A goal deposit comes out bigger than Zed can afford each month. The rate cannot change. Which change makes the deposit smaller?
questions.hint: Remember what the table of three waits showed.

options.text: Make the goal amount larger
options.why: A larger goal needs larger deposits.

options.text: Give the goal more months
options.why: More months spread the goal over more deposits, and interest has longer to help.

options.text: Cut the number of months
options.why: Fewer months mean bigger deposits, not smaller ones.

questions.label: Interest earned
questions.prompt: Lou puts $250.00 a month into an account paying 3% a year for 36 months. The balance at the end is $9,405.14. How many dollars of that balance came from interest?
questions.hint: Total deposits is the deposit times the months.
questions.why: The balance is the deposits plus the interest, so interest is the balance minus the deposits.
questions.miss: Work out how much Lou put in altogether, then take that from the balance.

traps.why: That is what Lou deposited. Interest is the balance minus that.

levels.title: Registered accounts and tax
learn: Say what an RRSP is and work out the room it gives you.
Tell how interest, dividends and capital gains are taxed outside a registered account, and what a tax shelter does.

cards.text: A registered account is an account set up under government rules, and it can hold investments. The account is the box and the investment is what is inside. A GIC is an investment. An RRSP is an account, so a GIC can sit in one. An RRSP is for saving toward retirement.

Your RRSP room is how much you may put in this year and deduct. It is 18% of last year’s earned income, up to a yearly maximum the CRA posts. If last year’s earned income was $60,000.00, the room is $10,800.00 (under the maximum). In your first year of earning there is no room yet: room comes from last year’s income.

The trade: money put in is a deduction, so it comes off your income before tax. Put in $5,000.00 and $48,000.00 of income is taxed as $43,000.00. The other side: money taken out is added to your income and taxed that year as income, and the room you used is not given back.

So an RRSP has two sides. An advantage is a deduction now and tax put off while the money grows. A disadvantage is tax later, when it comes out. It is not always better because of the deduction. It depends on your tax rate when you put money in, compared with when you take it out.

Outside a registered account, income from investments is taxed. Interest is taxed every year. A dividend, a share of a company’s profit paid to its owners, is taxed in the year you get it. A capital gain, selling for more than you paid, is taxed only when you sell. Rates are for the tax lessons.

A tax shelter holds an investment so that tax is put off or removed. An RRSP shelters money until it is cashed in. A TFSA is another registered account: money comes out tax-free, and the room comes back on January 1 of the next year. The choice depends on when you need the money.

questions.label: Room from income
questions.prompt: Pia’s earned income last year was $52,500.00. Her RRSP room is 18% of it, and that is less than the yearly maximum. How much room does she have?

terms.meaning: How much you may put into an RRSP this year and deduct.

questions.hint: Multiply last year’s earned income by 0.18.
questions.why: Room is 18% of last year’s earned income, when that is under the maximum.
questions.miss: Take 18% of last year’s earned income: multiply by 0.18.

questions.label: A first job
questions.prompt: Ari starts his first job in March this year. He had no earned income last year. How much RRSP room does this year give him?

terms.meaning: How much you may put into an RRSP this year and deduct.

questions.hint: Which year’s income is the room built from?

options.text: None yet, because room comes from last year’s earned income
options.why: Room is worked out from last year’s income, and last year it was nothing.

options.text: 18% of what he earns this year
options.why: This year’s income builds room for later years, not for this one.

options.text: The yearly maximum, for any new worker
options.why: The maximum is only a limit on the room. Room still has to come from earned income.

questions.label: Over the maximum
questions.prompt: Uma earned a lot last year, so 18% of her earned income is more than the yearly maximum. What is her room this year?

terms.meaning: How much you may put into an RRSP this year and deduct.

questions.hint: Look for the words “up to a yearly maximum”.

options.text: 18% of her income, since that is the rule
options.why: The rule says up to a yearly maximum, so 18% cannot go past it.

options.text: The yearly maximum, the smaller of the two
options.why: Room is 18% of last year’s earned income, up to the maximum. When 18% is bigger, the maximum applies.

options.text: Nothing, because her income is too high
options.why: A high income does not remove room. It only means the maximum applies.

questions.label: Income after deduction
questions.prompt: Teo’s income is $46,000.00. He puts $3,200.00 into an RRSP, within his room, and claims the deduction. What income is left to be taxed?

terms.meaning: An amount you may subtract from income before tax is worked out.

questions.hint: A deduction comes off income before tax is worked out.
questions.why: The RRSP money is a deduction, so it is subtracted from income before tax.
questions.miss: Subtract the amount put in from the income.

traps.why: That adds the deduction. A deduction is subtracted.

questions.label: Cashing in
questions.prompt: Years later Teo takes $8,000.00 out of the RRSP in a year when his other income is $39,500.00. How much income does that year show for tax?

terms.meaning: A registered account for saving toward retirement. Money put in is a deduction, and money taken out is taxed as income.

questions.hint: Money taken out of an RRSP is added to income that year.
questions.why: Money cashed in from an RRSP is taxed as income, so it is added to the other income.
questions.miss: Money taken out of an RRSP counts as income. Add it to the other income.

traps.why: That leaves out the money taken out. It is added to income.

questions.label: Gain timing
questions.prompt: Wen bought a share for $400.00. It is now worth $520.00 and Wen has not sold it. Outside a registered account, when is the capital gain taxed?

terms.meaning: The amount you sell something for, minus what you paid for it, when the price is higher.

questions.hint: Look at the table row for a capital gain.

options.text: Every year, like interest
options.why: Interest is taxed every year. A capital gain waits for the sale.

options.text: Right now, because the share is worth more
options.why: A higher price alone does not trigger tax. The sale does.

options.text: Only when Wen sells it
options.why: A capital gain is taxed when you sell. Until then it is a gain on paper.

questions.label: Which payment
questions.prompt: A company pays Mara $0.40 for each share she owns, out of its profit. What is this payment called?

terms.meaning: A share of a company’s profit paid out to its owners.

questions.hint: She owns shares, and the money comes out of profit.

options.text: A dividend
options.why: A dividend is a share of a company’s profit paid to its owners.

options.text: Interest
options.why: Interest is paid on money lent or saved. A share makes Mara an owner, not a lender.

options.text: A capital gain
options.why: A capital gain comes from selling for more than she paid. Nothing was sold here.

questions.label: Inside an RRSP
questions.prompt: Yara holds a GIC inside her RRSP for 10 years. When is the interest it earned taxed?

terms.meaning: A way of holding an investment so that tax is put off or removed.

questions.hint: An RRSP shelters money until it is cashed in.

options.text: Every year, as the interest is earned
options.why: That is how interest is taxed outside a registered account. An RRSP puts it off.

options.text: When she takes the money out of the RRSP, as income
options.why: The RRSP shelters it until it is cashed in, and then it is taxed as income.

options.text: Never, because the money comes out tax-free
options.why: Tax-free withdrawals belong to a TFSA. RRSP money is taxed as income when it comes out.

questions.label: Closest to $8,000
questions.prompt: Each bar is a person’s earned income last year. Everyone’s room is 18% of it, under the maximum. Tap the person whose room is closest to $8,000.00.

terms.meaning: How much you may put into an RRSP this year and deduct.

questions.hint: Multiply each income by 0.18, then compare with $8,000.00.
questions.miss: Work out 18% of each bar, then see which result is nearest $8,000.00.

levels.title: Does that number smell right?
learn: Turn a yearly return into a doubling time to check a number you found online.
Say what to do when a number looks wrong, and why a short good stretch is not a promise.

cards.text: Anyone can post a number about investing, and sites copy each other. Before you use a return you found online, ask three things. Where does it come from? How old is it? Is it a yearly rate? A number with no source and no date is a claim, not yet a fact.

A quick check is the sniff test. Turn the yearly return into a doubling time with the Rule of 72 (72 / rate) and see whether it looks sensible next to other sources. In this example, three sources put a savings account at 2% to 4% a year. That is a doubling time of 18 to 36 years.
Here are three typed returns for that savings account. Two land outside the range of other sources. Outside the range does not mean wrong. It means look again.

figure.title: Doubling time for a savings account

cards.text: When a number lands outside the range, open the source again. Did you copy the yearly rate, or a monthly rate or a total over 5 years? A page might say 0.4% per month, and 0.4 typed as a yearly rate gives 180 years. A yearly rate is about the monthly rate x 12. Fix a copying mistake.

If the page still shows the number, keep it and write “checked twice” beside it. Do not change a correctly sourced number to make it fit. That swaps a real figure for a guess. The test tells you where to look again. It does not tell you what the number should be.

A very short doubling time is a flag too. By the rule, under 6 years means a return above 12% a year (72 / 12 = 6). Write “past, not promised” beside it. A fund that did well for a few years shows what happened in those years, not what a 30-year plan can count on.

questions.label: Claim or fact
questions.prompt: Ina finds “funds return 15% a year” on a page with no author, no date and no source. What is it, as the cards put it?
questions.hint: Look at the first card: source, date and yearly rate.

options.text: A claim, not yet a fact
options.why: With no source and no date there is nothing to check it against.

options.text: A fact, because it is on the internet
options.why: Sites copy each other, so being online proves nothing.

options.text: A fact, because it is a number
options.why: A number can be wrong. It needs a source and a date.

questions.label: Doubling time
questions.prompt: A page lists a savings account at 0.5% a year. By the Rule of 72, how long until money doubles?

terms.meaning: A quick estimate: years to double is about 72 divided by the yearly rate in percent.

questions.hint: Divide 72 by the rate.

options.text: About 14.4 years
options.why: That divides by 5 instead of by 0.5. Divide 72 by the rate as written, 0.5.

options.text: About 36 years
options.why: That multiplies 72 by the rate. The rule divides.

options.text: About 144 years

questions.label: First step
questions.prompt: In this example other sources put a savings account at 2% to 4%, a doubling time of 18 to 36 years. Ina’s sheet shows 144 years. What is her first step?

terms.meaning: A quick check of whether a number looks sensible before you use it.

questions.hint: The test says look again, not change.

options.text: Change the rate to 3% so it fits the range
options.why: A fit-the-range change swaps a real figure for a guess.

options.text: Open the source again and check the rate it shows
options.why: The sniff test says where to look again. The page may show a monthly rate or a total.

options.text: Delete the row because it is wrong
options.why: Outside the range does not mean wrong. Check the source first.

questions.label: Rate from years
questions.prompt: A bond fund’s row shows money doubling in 16 years. By the Rule of 72, about what yearly rate is that?

terms.meaning: A quick estimate: years to double is about 72 divided by the yearly rate in percent.

questions.hint: The rule runs backwards: divide 72 by the years.
questions.why: The rate is about 72 divided by the years to double.
questions.miss: Divide 72 by the number of years, not the other way around.

traps.why: That multiplies. The rule divides 72 by the years.

questions.label: Monthly to yearly
questions.prompt: A page says a savings account pays 0.35% per month. Rey typed 0.35 as the yearly rate. About what yearly rate does the page show? Multiply the monthly rate by 12.
questions.hint: There are 12 months in a year.
questions.why: A monthly rate is about a twelfth of the yearly rate, so the yearly rate is about 12 times it.
questions.miss: The page gives one month. Multiply by the number of months in a year.

traps.why: That divides. A year has more months than one, so the yearly rate is bigger.

questions.label: Keep or change
questions.prompt: Eli checks the page twice. It still says 9% a year for a bond fund, outside the 3% to 5% her other sources give in this example. What do the cards say to do?
questions.hint: Look at the card on what to do if the page still shows the number.

options.text: Change it to 5% so it sits in the range
options.why: Changing a sourced number to fit the range is worse than the first mistake.

options.text: Remove the fund from her list
options.why: An unusual number is not a reason to drop the fund. It is a reason to look twice.

options.text: Keep 9% and write “checked twice” beside it
options.why: A correctly sourced number stays. The note shows she looked again.

questions.label: Fails the test
questions.prompt: In this example a savings account should double in 18 to 36 years. Each bar is a typed yearly rate. Tap the one whose doubling time falls outside that range.

terms.meaning: A quick check of whether a number looks sensible before you use it.

questions.hint: Divide 72 by each rate and compare with 18 to 36 years.
questions.why: 0.4% gives 72 / 0.4 = 180 years, far outside 18 to 36. The others give 22.5, 34.29, 18.95 years, all inside.
questions.miss: Work out 72 / rate for each bar. One result is far outside 18 to 36.

questions.label: Short stretch
questions.prompt: A page says a stock fund doubled in 4 years. Cal wants a rate for a 30-year plan. What do the cards say?

terms.meaning: A quick estimate: years to double is about 72 divided by the yearly rate in percent.

questions.hint: Turn 4 years into a yearly rate, then think about how short the stretch is.

options.text: That is about 18% a year over a short stretch, so mark it “past, not promised”
options.why: A doubling time under 6 years is a flag. A short stretch is not what a 30-year plan can count on.

options.text: Use it, since the newest number is the best
options.why: Recent is not the same as reliable. A short stretch is past, not promised.

options.text: Ignore the fund, since that return cannot be true
options.why: The number may be real for that stretch. It is just not a promise.

questions.label: Past growth
questions.prompt: A made-up fund grew 12% a year for the last 5 years. Multiply $5,000.00 by 1.12 five times. How much would it be after 5 years, to the nearest dollar?
questions.hint: Multiply by 1.12 once for each year.
questions.why: Each year multiplies the balance by 1.12. This shows what the money would have done, not what comes next.
questions.miss: Multiply by 1.12, five times in a row.

traps.why: That adds 12% of $5,000 each year. Interest is on the growing balance, so it is more.
